prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency
for the conception of the IceCube observatory and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube first and I have moved the optical lattice clock to the centre of my proposal after reading the ballots. B049 is the only shortlisted candidate that six of eight members ranked, with two first places and four top-three placements, and the support comes from members with very different tastes. Its case is what I look for as an instrument builder: a clear idea (the magic wavelength that cancels the light shift), a realisation that moved fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18, and independent confirmation from many laboratories, including remote clock comparisons across continents. It opens relativistic geodesy, tests of constants and dark-matter couplings, and a possible redefinition of the second. The attribution is the cleanest on the list, a natural pair in Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for taking the performance to the record. I keep B047 as a second, distinct part because high-energy neutrino astronomy is a real new observational window. A cubic-kilometre detector in the Antarctic ice saw a diffuse astrophysical flux in 2013. That flux has been corroborated in several channels, and it is now tied to TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane. It also brings a different field to the table than atomic and condensed-matter physics, which a two-part prize can accommodate.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection to my own configuration is B047. Halzen is the only credited name for a collaboration of hundreds, and I cannot show from the supplied material that a single person is the decisive credit; a committee could reasonably say the discovery belongs to the collaboration or to a wider set of leaders, and a one-person part invites dispute. I also must count my own field affinity as a bias, since only Ulf Danielsson and I ranked B047 at all, so my enthusiasm is not evidence of committee support. Source identification (NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) is statistically more modest than the diffuse flux, although the diffuse flux itself is secure. For B049, Hall and Hansch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already covered the comb and ion-clock groundwork, so some members may see the lattice clock as an incremental step on prior prizes, and the second has not yet been redefined. If B047 cannot be sustained on attribution, the right fallback is B049 alone or B049 with B024, not a weaker second part.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first because the idea is original, performance is unambiguous and confirmed by many independent groups (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE), and it enables further work across physics.
responses.response: I agree, and it is what moved me towards B049. For me the decisive feature is that the systematics are understood and reproduced in several laboratories, with clocks now compared between sites, so the result will last. Where I would qualify your argument is the precision-first framing. It is the magic-wavelength concept plus the demonstrated 1e-18 accuracy that earns the prize, not precision alone, and the citation should say so. I also note that your atom-interferometry ranking (B020) is a fair rival for the instrument-driven slot, but its headline fundamental-physics results are still developing, so I rank it below the clock.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B049 first as a genuine conceptual step beyond single-ion clocks, with Katori proposing the magic-wavelength scheme and Ye bringing clocks to the 1e-18 level, and she finds the two-person credit natural.
responses.response: I agree on both the physics and the credit, and as an atomic-physics specialist you are better placed than I am to say whether Ye's many-body and density-shift studies belong in the citation as well as the accuracy record. My view is that the citation should name the lattice-clock concept and its realisation, and not enumerate applications, because the redefinition of the second is still pending. I would not make that a precondition, since confirmation by comparisons between laboratories is already strong. Your remark that B054 and B044 compete for the same theorists (Zoller, Cirac) is a useful warning against splitting support across those ballots.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the theta-13 reactor result first as a clean, unambiguous discovery from nature that opens CP-violation searches, and B047 third, while noting that Halzen alone is a thin basis for a collaboration-scale discovery and that Double Chooz leadership is missing from B024.
responses.response: Your reservation about Halzen's sole credit is the strongest point against my own opening, and I accept it as a real weakness: it is why I hold B047 only as a second part and would drop it if the committee cannot document his decisive role. On B024 I agree it is a precise, mature, independently confirmed result and I keep it as an alternative. I do not make it my main choice for two reasons. The credit is spread across Daya Bay, RENO and Double Chooz, and a prize for neutrino oscillations was given in 2015, so the committee would need to explain why theta-13 is a distinct achievement. That argument can be made, but I think it is harder than for the clocks.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first as theory tested against real band structures, with fifteen years of confirmation, and sees it as arguably overdue.
responses.response: I find the maturity argument persuasive, and condensed matter is outside my expertise, so I defer to you and Mehlig on the physics. My difficulty is attribution: you and Danielsson both note that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe mechanism that Molenkamp's group then tested, and the supplied names omit them. A prize for B048 would need that credit question resolved, or the committee would be accused of a gap. I keep it as an alternative because three members rank it highly and the science is solid.

uncertainties: Whether Francis Halzen alone can be credited for the IceCube discovery, or whether the committee would need a different or broader set of names that are not on the supplied ballot.
Whether a two-part prize combining a metrology prize with neutrino astronomy is acceptable to colleagues, or whether B049 should stand alone with a stronger consensus.
Whether the remaining pending redefinition of the SI second affects the timing of B049, and whether Ye's many-body clock work belongs in the citation.
Whether B024 is distinct enough from the 2015 neutrino-oscillation prize, and how much weight to give the omission of Double Chooz leadership.
statement.conflict_note: I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and am a professor of astroparticle physics, so B047 (IceCube) and B024 (neutrinos) are close to my own field and I may favour them; I have no direct connection to IceCube, Daya Bay, RENO or the lattice-clock groups apparent from my profile, but I flag this field affinity and would accept recusal on B047 if colleagues consider it necessary.
